source_terms: Audio brand mentions enhance onscreen brand visuals' performance
Supercharge your brand visual performance with audio brand mentions
item.claim: The source claims an interaction rather than an addition: an audio mention of the brand raises the performance of the on-screen brand visual it accompanies. The instruction is to pair the two, not to choose between them.

scope.conditions: YouTube, where the source states audio is almost always heard

caveats.text: "Enhance ... performance" is a performance claim with no figure, no measure and no study attached at this level. The named study behind the page's headline lift is not decomposed by principle, so nothing quantifies this particular claim.

The claim depends on the audio actually being heard, which the source asserts for YouTube specifically. On a surface where audio is off by default the claim's premise does not hold, and the source neither says so nor addresses any other surface.

Platform- and time-contingent. This is guidance about one company's ad products on one platform. Playback behaviour, ad formats and surfaces change; the source does not claim a durable mechanism and none should be read in.

Declared publisher interest. The publisher sells advertising on the platform whose creative guidance this is, and the cited research validates that product. Third-party involvement (Ipsos as research partner; Nielsen and Kantar as independent reviewers, per the source's own account) moderates this; it does not remove it.

source_stated_remedies: Supercharge your brand visual performance with audio brand mentions

positive.description: Oi reinforces its on-screen brand visuals with a corresponding spoken brand mention

intra_source_relations.note: the claim assumes the audio is heard
the same pair-audio-with-picture move applied to the CTA

item.source_locator: Google Ads Help, section "Core ABCDs", row "Branding", guideline "Reinforce with audio"; Google for Business resources, section "B – Branding", sub-heading "See and say"
item.question: What exactly does the source claim about audio brand mentions, and is it an additive claim or an interactive one?
item.answer: Interactive. The claim is that "Audio brand mentions enhance onscreen brand visuals' performance" — the spoken mention raises the performance of the visual it accompanies, rather than contributing a separate increment of its own. That is why the instruction is to pair the two ("see and say") rather than to choose between them. It is a performance claim with nothing attached: no figure, no measure, no study at this level, and the headline lift the pages carry is stated for the ABCDs as a set and never decomposed by principle. The claim also presupposes the audio is heard, which the source asserts for YouTube and for nothing else.
item.support: The verb is "enhance ... performance", applied to the on-screen visual. No quantity is given at either locator.
confounders: reading it as 'audio branding also works', which is the additive reading and loses the interaction
attaching part of the 30% lift to this technique; the source never decomposes the figure
assuming a mechanism is given; the source states the effect and not the cause

item.source_title: Google, "ABCDs of effective video ads" — Google Ads Help, Google for Business resources and Think with Google (retrieved 30 August 2026)
item.source_locator: Google Ads Help, section "Benefits" and its source note; section "Core ABCDs", row "Branding", guideline "Reinforce with audio"
item.question: A planner wants to argue that adding a spoken brand mention on its own will deliver most of the 30% short-term sales lift. Can this source support that argument?
item.answer: No, on three counts. The lift figures are stated for "the ABCDs" as a set on all three pages and are never decomposed by principle, still less by individual technique, so no share of the 30% can be assigned to anything. The source's only claim about audio brand mentions is qualitative — that they enhance the on-screen brand visual's performance — with no figure attached at all. And the set-level number itself is unstable across the publisher's own pages, appearing as an upper bound on one and as an average on another, so it will not carry a per-campaign expectation even before anyone tries to split it.
item.support: The lift is attached to the ABCDs as a set at the Benefits locator; the audio guideline carries no quantity.
confounders: apportioning the lift across the four principles, or across techniques, as if the source had reported components
reading 'enhance performance' as a quantified uplift
using the 'on average' phrasing from one page as a per-campaign expectation

item.source_locator: Ch. 1, section 'subject, style, speed, locality', printed pp. 58-61
item.question: What are the regional iconographic codes described here, and what role do they play in whether an image is accepted?
item.answer: They are a well-defined regional iconography — reported consistently by artists, printers, distributors and clients — operating not only at the level of which deities are favoured but at the level of their attributes and formal treatment. Jain's enumerated examples: Lakshmi and Shiva preferred standing in the north and seated in the south; the eyes of Shiva and Hanuman wide open in the south and often half-closed in the north; Ganesh's ears and trunk longer in the north, his face paler in Bengal; Lakshmi accompanied by an owl in Bengal and nowhere else; Radha often portrayed with her garments askew in the north, while in Bengal all goddesses are covered to the point that even their ears are hidden. Their role is that they are THE MAIN GROUND OF REJECTION: artists develop a thorough knowledge of the codes because accuracy in following them is a particularly stringent requirement, and getting one wrong is what gets a design turned back. Note the direction of the reported evidence, which the source is clear about: the codes are reported by the trade as things it must satisfy, and the acceptance behaviour is the trade's.
item.support: accuracy in following the regional codes is 'a particularly stringent' requirement
item.confounders: The enumerated list looks like a code that could be turned into a checkable specification. Jain reports illustrative examples from informants, not a complete or dated code, and reports no survey of prints against it.
